newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe rejects cabinet change, early vote.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe rejects cabinet change, early vote.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe rejected on Tuesday a call by a senior politician in his ruling coalition for a cabinet reshuffle, early elections or a referendum to stem rising discontent in France.

Francois Leotard, head of the Union for French Democracy (UDF) junior coalition partner, had urged President Jacques Chirac at the weekend to choose one of the three options for a society he called "wounded, emotional and sceptical".
An opinion poll released on Tuesday, meanwhile, showed that 96 percent of French voters felt "anxious" or "morose" about the economic and social situation.

However Gilles de Robien, floor leader of the UDF (Union for French Democracy) in the National Assembly, said Juppe had told a meeting of UDF parliamentarians that he believed such shock treatment as Leotard proposed was not justified.

"Alain Juppe said parliament could not be dissolved unless there was a serious crisis, that a cabinet reshuffle could not be carried out without serious thought and there must be a good subject to organise a referendum," de Robien said.

The popularity of Chirac and Juppe has fallen to near-record lows in the face of a stagnating economy, record unemployment and budget austerity imposed to help France meet criteria to join a planned single European currency from 1999.

The UDF has recently stepped up criticism of Juppe's policies in the long run-up to the next general election in 1988. The UDF and Juppe's Gaullist Rally for the Republic party have an overwhelming majority in parliament.

Yet the public mood is very downbeat. The BVA poll for the weekly magazine Paris Match showed that 74 percent of those questioned felt anxiety and 22 percent were morose while only three percent were confident about the current state of affairs in France, where unemployment is at a record high of 12.6 percent.
In addition, 67 percent of participants said they did not believe there would be an economic recovery in 1997, compared to 23 percent who did.

A huge majority -- 73 percent against 14 percent -- reckoned that Prime Minister Alain Juppe was wrong to say there was no alternative to his policy of giving priority to cutting public deficits before reducing unemployment.
